summary: For ages 7–9, teach the three-way classification of volcanoes — active (erupting or likely to erupt), dormant (long-quiet but could reawaken), extinct (thought to have no remaining magma supply, so not expected to erupt again) — by reasoning from eruption-history and monitoring EVIDENCE against a volcano's very long lifespan. The load-bearing idea to dislodge is that dormant does NOT mean safe/dead: centuries of quiet is a blink on a volcano's timescale, so a long-silent volcano can still be dormant. Classification is judged from history and evidence, not the mountain's appearance.
misconceptions: Dormant means safe/dead (dormant volcanoes can and do reawaken — they are only sleeping).
A volcano that hasn't erupted in a long time (even centuries) must be extinct (that can still be dormant on a volcano's time-scale).
Active means constantly erupting (active means erupting OR likely to erupt — it can be quiet between eruptions).
You can tell status just by looking at the mountain's shape (status is judged from eruption history and monitoring evidence, not appearance).
Extinct volcanoes can suddenly come back (truly extinct = no magma supply; the risk is mistaking a dormant one for extinct).

activities.title: Volcano-sorting bench: classify by evidence, with a planted surprise
steps: Sort a deck of volcano cards into three bins — active, dormant, extinct — using each card's eruption-history timeline and monitoring clues (last eruption date, gas/ground-swelling signs, whether a magma supply is present).

Include one 'trap' card: a volcano silent for 400 years that many learners may file as 'extinct'. Make sure its card evidence points to dormant if read carefully (for example, a history of eruptions separated by long gaps and no evidence that its magma supply has ended), so the reveal is fair. After they commit, reveal that it erupts again — showing it was dormant (capable of erupting) all along and never truly extinct — with the line 'quiet for a long time isn't the same as finished.'
Use a time-scale slider (optional interaction) to compare human lifetimes — 'no eruption in your grandparents' lifetime' — against the volcano's age, showing that 400 years is a blink.
State for each card WHY you chose a bin, pointing to the specific evidence rather than the mountain's shape or greenery.
activities.insight: Volcano status is a judgement from eruption history and monitoring evidence measured against a very long lifespan; a long-quiet volcano may be dormant, not extinct, and dormant is not the same as dead or safe.

activities.title: Consolidation: categorise and judge from evidence blurbs
steps: Read short evidence blurbs for several volcanoes and sort each into active, dormant, or extinct.
Answer a reasoning question: 'A volcano hasn't erupted in 300 years — is it definitely extinct?' and justify the answer ('no — it could still be dormant').
Explain in your own words the difference between dormant and extinct, and what evidence would help decide if a volcano is truly extinct.
activities.insight: Learners can apply the three categories to new cases and recognise that long quiet alone does not prove extinction.

activities.title: Example trio with 'sleeping vs never-waking' reveal
steps: Examine three example volcanoes, one of each status, each with a short eruption-history/monitoring summary, and predict the status of each FROM that evidence — not from the mountain's appearance — before revealing it.
For the dormant example, answer 'Could this sleeping one wake up?' and then reveal: 'Yes — dormant means asleep, not gone.'
Discuss the 'sleeping vs never-waking' metaphor: dormant = asleep and can wake; extinct = not expected to wake because its magma supply seems to be gone.
activities.insight: The categories map onto a memorable metaphor — asleep (dormant, can wake) versus never-waking (extinct) — anchored to concrete examples and judged from evidence rather than looks.

activities.title: Ask a volcanologist: how do we decide dormant vs extinct?
steps: Pose or discuss questions a volcanologist would answer: 'How do you decide if a volcano is dormant or extinct?' and 'What evidence do you use?'
Explore why extinct is the hardest call to make, and that scientists work with uncertainty.
Connect to monitoring (bridge toward later study of how volcanoes are monitored and people are warned).
activities.insight: Deciding status relies on evidence and expert judgement, and classifying something as truly extinct is genuinely uncertain.

checkQuestion: A volcano hasn't erupted for 400 years and is covered in trees and grass. A friend says, 'It's clearly dead — it will never erupt again, so it must be extinct.' Do you agree? How would you classify this volcano, and what would you need to know to be sure?
checkAnswer: Not necessarily — being quiet for a long time and looking green doesn't mean it's dead. A volcano that could still erupt again is dormant ('sleeping'), not extinct. Extinct means it will not erupt again. To classify it you'd look at its eruption history and whether scientists think its magma supply is finished — 400 silent years alone doesn't prove extinction.
